content.text:
Coningsby refuses Lord Monmouth’s demand that he contest Darlford, choosing conscience over privilege and Parliament. After Lord Monmouth separates from Lucretia, dies, and leaves his fortune to Flora, Coningsby loses his inheritance, visits Flora at her Brook Street hotel, studies law in the Temple, and renounces Edith. Millbank later nominates him at Darlford; Coningsby travels with Oswald to Birmingham, then Darlford, wins the election, reunites with Edith, and marries her at Millbank. Flora subsequently dies and leaves him her fortune.

The text then surveys railroad disasters—collisions, derailments, fires, bridge and drawbridge failures—and argues that disciplined investigation, interlocking signals, automatic electric blocks, stronger cars, and continuous automatic brakes greatly improve safety. Despite spectacular accidents, statistical evidence shows rail travel is extraordinarily safe, especially compared with stagecoaches and everyday urban hazards. The closing poems mourn lost beloveds and affirm enduring fidelity.
